title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction: Setting: a thin elastic lamina (cantilever) clamped in a wall over a short embedded portion Aa (A and a are two points of the embedded part, in Euler's Tab. VII), free at the far end F, vibrating transversely. Here x is position along the lamina, y(x,t) the transverse displacement, K/k the mass per unit length, and 1/(2b) a unit-conversion factor from Euler's convention for time units. On the previous page Euler showed that the element dx at Y must carry the motive force YV = (K dx/2bk)(d²y/dt²) for the assumed motion to occur. The only real external forces are those the wall exerts on the clamped portion. Section VI argues that one force applied at A, however large, cannot resist bending. A second, oppositely directed force at a, acting together with the first, can. In modern terms, a clamped end supplies both a shear force and a bending moment (a couple), not just a point force. Euler stresses that the sizes of these two reactions are unknown in advance and vary with the state of the lamina; the solution will determine them, and so the load the wall bears at each instant. Section VII applies d'Alembert's principle. Requiring the elementary forces to be equivalent to the two wall forces is the same as requiring the reversed forces −(K dx/2bk)(d²y/dt²), applied to every point Y, to be in equilibrium with the wall forces at A and a. The dynamic problem thus becomes a static one, and the motion itself no longer has to be considered. Continuing onto the next page: cut the lamina at Y and look at the free part YF, which carries only the reversed inertial loads p dx. Their moment about Y must equal the elastic moment Kc²·y''. Differentiating twice then gives the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation, Kc²·y'''' = −(K/2bk)·y_tt, in Euler's units. This page is the conceptual set-up for that equation.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The argument is qualitative and correct: a clamped support must be modelled as a force plus a couple (two opposed forces at A and a), and d'Alembert's reversal of the inertial forces turns the problem into one of statics. (Side note on the next page's transcription: the elastic moment is printed or transcribed as Kcc(ddy/dt²); in context it should be the curvature, Kcc(ddy/dx²).)

ideas.what: A clamped (built-in) end cannot be represented by a single point force. It needs two opposed forces at points A and a of the embedded part, i.e. a force plus a couple, whose magnitudes are unknown reactions found from the solution.
ideas.modern_name: Clamped boundary reaction: shear force plus bending moment (fixed-end moment)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Jakob/Daniel Bernoulli and Euler's earlier elastica and beam-vibration work (1740s); standard in later beam theory (Navier 1820s)
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier vibration and elastica work, e.g. E65 (Additamentum De curvis elasticis, 1744) and the 1730s–40s papers on vibrating laminae (Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies, 1960)

ideas.what: Reversed inertial forces applied to each element are set in equilibrium with the external (wall) forces, reducing the dynamical problem to one of statics.
ideas.where_published: Used throughout Euler's mechanics, e.g. vibrating-string and lamina papers; discussed in Truesdell 1960

ideas.what: Balance of moments, about a point Y, of the reversed inertial loads on the free segment YF against the elastic moment Kc²y''; this leads to the fourth-order beam vibration equation.
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Bernoulli dynamic beam equation (derived via cut-section moment balance)
ideas.where_published: E40 (1735), E65 (1744), and this paper E443 (Novi Comm. Petrop. 17, 1772/1773)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard expository set-up of d'Alembert's principle and of the clamped-end reaction (force plus couple). Truesdell's historical account of Euler's beam-vibration work covers both thoroughly, and nothing on the page is new or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: Line 'nondum fumus folliciti': the image is smudged ('fumus ...liciti'), but 'solliciti' is the right reading.
Otherwise the transcription matches the image; the formula is YV = (K dx/2bk)(d²y/dt²), as printed both times.
